citation: Currey, J. Seymour. The Story of Old Fort Dearborn. Chicago: A. C. McClurg & Co., 1912.
author: J. Seymour Currey
describes_date: 1779-1816; the passage cited here describes the Kinzie house from 1804
repository: Project Gutenberg eBook #52346 (released 16 June 2016), transcribed from the 1912 edition
locator: ch. II, 'Fortifying the Frontier', the paragraphs before the plate 'Residence of John Kinzie' (facing p. 32 by the volume's list of illustrations)
rights_note: Published 1912 in the United States, out of copyright by age; Project Gutenberg distributes it as a public-domain text.
access_notes: Read on 2026-10-15 (T-2497) from the Gutenberg plain-text file https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/52346/pg52346.txt, fetched from the run's container. The page numbers of the printed book are not carried by the transcription; the locator is the chapter and the plate the passage stands beside. The sand-dune passage in ch. II was read from the same Gutenberg text on 2026-10-17 for the 1812/1835 tree research (/mnt/project-files/trees-1812-1835/sources.md F1).
what_it_supplies: the house's builder, Jean Baptiste Point de Saible, 'a native of San Domingo and a negro', and that he built it 'some time before 1779' near the present foot of Pine Street
its sale in 1797 to Le Mai, and Le Mai's sale to John Kinzie in 1804, Kinzie arriving 'in the fall of that year'
Kinzie's work on it: 'he repaired it, added a veranda, and planted four Lombardy poplars at the foot of the slope on which the house stood'
its orientation: 'The house faced toward the south, having the river directly in front and the lake a short distance to the east'
that it 'escaped the general destruction at the time of the massacre' and 'was finally demolished in the early thirties'
Ouilmette's cabin 'close in the rear of the Kinzie house' and Pettell's 'small cabin near the Kinzie house'

the lake shore south of the river mouth before 1812, in the same chapter: 'mostly devoid of trees, a scanty growth of cottonwoods and pines, however, maintaining a precarious existence among the sand-dunes', the low sand-hills 'the predominant feature of the landscape' a mile or two south of the mouth (used by T-2768 for the pines on the south sand hills)
what_it_does_not_supply: any dimension of the house, the piazza or the green
the number of the house's rooms, windows or chimneys
a date for the veranda or the poplars more exact than 'after the house came into the possession of John Kinzie'
the Sarony lithograph itself: the Gutenberg file carries only its caption, so the plate is not read here
note: A secondary history written a century after the events, so tier 3. Its dates for Le Mai (1797) and Kinzie (1804) differ from Moses and Kirkland's (1796; Kinzie's arrival given elsewhere as 1803), and the Kinzie house record carries both. The Sarony plate's caption reads: 'The house in which John Kinzie and his family lived from 1804 to 1813, and again from 1816 to 1828, as it was lithographed by Sarony from a sketch made by Mrs. John H. Kinzie, the author of Wau-Bun.'
